The diagram above shows the graph of $y=k{log}_{2}⁡(bx).$ Find the value of $k\cdot b.$
questions.worked_solution:
Clearly, $b\ne 0.$ Substituting $x=\frac{1}{b}$ into the equation of the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{2}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{2}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(\frac{1}{b},0)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(3,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence

$$
(3,0)=(\frac{1}{b},0)\,⇒\,b=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(6,2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{2}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{3}\cdot 6) & =2 \\ k{log}_{2}⁡2 & =2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
k\cdot b=2\cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The diagram above shows the graph of $y={log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c.$ Find the value of $\frac{d}{c}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In the given graph, the vertical asymptote is $x=4.$ So, the argument of the logarithm function should evaluate to zero at $x=4.$ Therefore,

$$
4-d=0\,⇒\,d=4.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(8,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(x-d)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(x-4)+c & =y \\ {log}_{4}⁡(8-4)+c & =3 \\ {log}_{4}⁡(4)+c & =3 \\ 1+c & =3 \\ c & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{d}{c}=\frac{4}{2}=2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Unknown Parameters Given a Transformed Logarithmic Function
canonical_examples.problem:
The diagram below shows the graph of $y=k \log_5 (bx).$ Find the value of $b\cdot k.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246252/assets/3698fc49edb443517ed0ee2cfa81c586c428f402df7028a8ec4b47702d8a4fad.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Clearly, $b \neq 0.$ Substituting $x=\dfrac1b$ into the equation of the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k{log}_{5}⁡(b\cdot \frac{1}{b}) \\  & =k{log}_{5}⁡1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $\left(\dfrac1b, 0\right)$ lies on the curve. But from the diagram, we know that $(2,0)$ lies on the curve. Hence, 

$$
(2,0)  = \left(\dfrac1b,0\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=\dfrac12.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(10,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{log}_{5}⁡(bx) & =y \\ k{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{1}{2}x) & =y \\ k{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10) & =3 \\ k{log}_{5}⁡5 & =3 \\ k & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
b\cdot k = \dfrac12 \cdot 3 = \dfrac32.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we are given the function

$$
y=5\log_6(x-2).
$$

How do we plot its graph?

As usual, we can do this by combining transformations of the curve $y=\log_6 x.$

- We start with the graph of $y=\log_6 x{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246252/assets/a85eb96e169e43568da76e33ee7f997af9196d26e867d7e7db1b2ddea0725d2a.png)

- Translate it by $2$ units to the right to get the graph of $y=\log_6{(x-2)}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246252/assets/248a60c13ac422aeace5ba19f9f25716b188c19dbe04f5970287c587adb44c85.png)

Notice that points $(1,0)$ and $(6,1)$ on the graph of $y=\log_6 x$ map to the points $(3,0)$ and $(8,1)$ on the graph of $y=\log_6 (x-2),$ respectively.

- Then, stretch the result by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of $y=5\log_6{(x-2)}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14246252/assets/a67b409068f67d81f0217aaeb30f76bd63c6501376d2adc567db7c4f319d7144.png)

So, to plot the curve of a transformed logarithmic function, we apply subsequent transformations presented in the given function, as usual.
